title: Anastasios N Angelopoulos - Agent Arena: Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World

I'm honored to be speaking here today.
I was a student at Berkeley not too long ago.
Actually, Arena started as a student project.
It was just-- I was a PhD student here.
I was working with Mike Jordan and Jitender Malik,
and we had this collaboration with Ion Stoica, who,
as you guys know, was the first CEO of Databricks
and also a professor here, that turned into the Arena.
All of the model labs started competing on our platform,
and now it's become a company, which has grown gangbusters
from there.
And so some of you might have seen it online.
But here, I'm going to tell you guys a little bit about how
we evaluate agents.
Of course, this is the conference for agents,
so it won't be any surprise to you.
But we recently released our new agent, Arena,
about seven weeks ago that has led
to millions and millions of users
online using agenst on arena.ai, and us
being able to extract organic signals of utility
to people for agentic tasks.
So with that, a little bit about Arena.
Arena is the evaluation company.
The purpose of arena is to say that static benchmarks
and so on.
They have a lot of flaws.
You can overfit them.
And then there's also, often, a distribution shift between what
you can collect a data set for and what
actually happens in production.
Arena works a little bit differently.
Our philosophy on evaluations is that there's only one judge that
matters, and that's reality.
Reality is actually the source of objective truth.
It's our way of measuring the post-deployment impacts
of models.
And it can't be gamed.
Because it's actually just in order to do well, in reality,
you needed to have real people's jobs,
and then be able to complete them successfully.
And so we measure intelligence in the real world.
And I'll tell you a little bit about the way that we do that.
Long story short, Arena has a consumer application,
which is arena.ai, that you guys can go visit today.
I'll tell you a little bit about it in a second.
But we collect two types of data on Arena
that we can turn into benchmarks.
I've shown the two up here on this slide.
The first type of data, which you might be familiar with Arena
for is pairwise preference data.
So that's one prompt, and then two responses,
and then the user votes for the better response.
Now this is not on the talk track,
but I'll tell you, guys, there's something
that I call the fundamental principle of arena,
which drives all of this.
The fundamental principle of arena
is that the act of providing feedback
should give value back to the user.
And that's what allows us to collect
millions and millions of data points
without having to pay people.
People are coming to the website and using it for free.
And then in doing so, they're giving us valuable feedback
that can turn into evaluations.
And the way that we give value back to the user,
through the voting mechanism, is that when
they vote for the response that they like better,
they continue with it in the chat.
So anybody that doesn't want to screw up their models context
is incentivized to vote their true preference.
And so this has led us to have quite a few high quality
votes on the platform.
The second type of data, which you might be unfamiliar with,
arena for collecting, is called trace mining data.
So here, it's away from the battle mechanism,
so it's one prompt, one response.
And then there's these long multi-turn conversations
happening over days and weeks on the platform,
that we can mine for signals.
So here, I've put an example of a user that architected
a rag financial brain.

what we do in our leaderboards.

the model, which allows us to then do causal inference.
And by causal inference, what I mean
is to say that you can think about,
let's say, the orchestrator in the agent or the tools
of the agent as a treatment.
And then try to measure the treatment
effect of what would happen if you used one
orchestrator versus another.
What happens if I use fable as my orchestrator model,

might be a randomized average of the rest of them.
And so that's what our leaderboards actually show.
If you go to arena.ai/leaderboard,
the default leaderboard that you'll see will be
the leaderboard, and it will be a treatment effect-based
leaderboard.
That runs basically large multi-factor A/B test experiment
on all the subcomponents of the agent.
And what we do is we compile that leaderboard out
of a bunch of different signals.
One of the signals is that task completion, yes/no, my task
was done or not, that you saw on the previous video.
But we also have all these other signals,
like praise versus complaint, which
is the fraction of positive versus negative feedback
that users are giving to the agent.
We also have hallucination rates.
We're stripping every factual claim,
and then using a bunch of search models
to go look along the internet to try
to see if we can verify that claim
or verify that it was incorrect.
Steerability, which is a user will say something,
the model will respond, and then as the user struggling
to do the same thing over and over again,
or the model like correctly land the fix after they initially
complained.
Bash recovery.
Is the model able to recover from errors
that it makes in bash?
Does it make errors in the first place?
All of these are very rich signals
that you can mine from organic data, and would be surprising.

models are not making errors at all because they've all
overfit to them.

So you can do that, and then you can
break these causal inference, these treatment
